title: Estius's answer: freedom requires choice from a judgment that could have been otherwise; only uncreated will has its choice from no prior
source_text: XXIII. Ad hoc vero respondet ad rationem liberi arbitrii; hoc sufficere, ut ex praevio judicio intellectus practici, sic eligat unum oppositorum, ut tamen ex ejusdem intellectus diverso judicio possit eligere alterum; quia, scilicet, radix & fundamentum libertatis arbitrii est in intellectu, quatenus ille diversas boni rationes circa opposita potest considerare, & voluntati proponere, rationem vero liberi arbitrii non includere, ut dum agens liberum ex judicio praevio eligit, ad sic judicandum atque eligendum non moveatur ab aliqua causa superiori. Ac proinde cum motio Dei voluntatem praedeterminans non impediat quominus homo plenum atque perfectum habeat judicium rationis, & judicet aliud medium esse contingens, aliud autem cum fine ex necessitate connexum, & posset quoque ex diverso judicio aliud eligere, hoc ipso, talem motionem libertati Voluntatis nostrae nihil officere. Quippe proprium esse Voluntatis increatae ut electionem suam ab aliquo priori non habeat.
pass_a_gloss: But to this he answers that for the nature of free choice; this suffices, that from a previous judgment of the practical intellect, it so choose one of opposites, that yet from a different judgment of the same intellect it could choose the other; because, namely, the root and foundation of liberty of choice is in the intellect, in so far as it can consider different reasons of good about opposites, and propose them to the will, but that the nature of free choice does not include, that while a free agent chooses from a previous judgment, it be not moved to so judging and choosing by some superior cause. And accordingly since the motion of God predetermining the will does not hinder that man have a full and perfect judgment of reason, and judge that one means is contingent, but another connected with the end by necessity, and that he could also choose another from a different judgment, by this very fact, such a motion does no harm to the liberty of our Will. Indeed it is proper to the uncreated Will that it does not have its choice from some prior.
pass_b_english: His answer is that for the nature of free choice it is enough that the will, on a prior judgment of the practical intellect, chooses one of two opposites in such a way that it could choose the other on a different judgment of the same intellect. The root and foundation of freedom of choice lies in the intellect, insofar as it can weigh different aspects of good in opposite options and set them before the will.

The nature of free choice does not require that a free agent, when it chooses on a prior judgment, should not be moved by some higher cause to judge and choose as it does. So, since God's motion predetermining the will does not prevent a man from having a full and complete judgment of reason, judging one means contingent and another necessarily connected with the end, and being able to choose differently on a different judgment, that motion does the freedom of our will no harm. It belongs only to the uncreated will not to receive its choice from something prior.

lemmas.gloss: the root and foundation of liberty

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
